## Method

### Data Analysis

**Scoring.** For each vignette, trust was scored as the mean of 10 items
(five trust items and five distrust items, the latter reverse-coded so that
higher scores indicate greater trust), and acceptance as the mean of four
items. Satisfaction was a single item. All three outcomes ranged from 1 to 5.

**Analytic sample and coding.** Analyses included all participants who
responded to at least one vignette (*N* = 58; 174 participant × vignette
observations). No outcome data were missing. Each participant was assigned to
the Asked condition (consent was requested before MedHelper acted) in some
vignettes and the Not asked condition (informed afterwards) in the others, so
condition varied both between participants within a vignette and within
participants across vignettes. Condition was coded 0 = Asked, 1 = Not asked,
so negative condition effects are in the hypothesized direction. All tests
were two-sided with α = .05. Holm's (1979) correction was applied within each
family of related tests (the nine between-participant comparisons in H1; the
three outcomes in each set of mixed models).

**Between-participant effects of condition (H1).** Within each vignette,
participants in the Asked and Not asked conditions were compared on each
outcome with Welch's *t* tests, which do not assume equal variances. Effect
sizes are Hedges' *g* computed with unpooled standard deviations, with 95% CIs.
Wilcoxon rank-sum tests were run as a nonparametric check.

**Within-participant effects of condition (H1).** Because each participant
contributed three observations, within-participant effects were estimated
with linear mixed models, with a random intercept for participant and vignette
entered as a fixed effect to absorb differences between vignettes (and their
fixed presentation order). To separate within- from between-participant
variation (Enders & Tofighi, 2007), the condition indicator was decomposed into
the participant's proportion of Not asked vignettes (between) and the
deviation from that proportion (within); the within-person coefficient is the
estimate of interest. Three follow-up analyses were conducted: (a) a
Condition × Vignette interaction, tested with an *F* test, to assess whether
the effect varied across vignettes; (b) equivalence tests using the two
one-sided tests procedure (TOST; Lakens, 2017), based on the 90% CI of the
within-person estimate, to assess whether any effect was negligibly small
[state the smallest effect size of interest and its justification]; and
(c) a carryover model, fitted to Vignettes 2 and 3, that added the condition
of the preceding vignette and its interaction with the current condition.

**Trust and acceptance as predictors of satisfaction (H2).** Satisfaction was
modeled as a function of trust and acceptance, each decomposed into a person
mean (between-participant component) and the deviation from that mean
(within-participant component), with condition and vignette as covariates and
a random intercept for participant. Trust and acceptance were entered first
separately and then jointly to estimate their unique contributions.
Multicollinearity was assessed with variance inflation factors (VIFs), and
variance explained with marginal and conditional *R*^2^ (Nakagawa &
Schielzeth, 2013).

**Exploratory analyses.** Among Asked vignettes, ratings were compared across
participants' responses to the two consent requests (consented to both,
consented to one, declined both) using mixed models of the same form, with
each group compared with "consented to both" (Holm-adjusted). To examine
whether differences reflected a general stance toward MedHelper, each
participant's consent rate (proportion of requests accepted) was used to
predict their ratings in Not asked vignettes, and a Consent Rate × Condition
interaction tested whether the association was stronger in Asked than in Not
asked vignettes. We also tested whether Not asked ratings were closer to those
of participants who consented than to those who declined, using the contrast
|Declined − Not asked| − |Consented − Not asked|. This was estimated in two
ways. At the group level, we used a linear model with vignette as a covariate
and cluster-robust (CR1) standard errors by participant. Relative to each
participant's own baseline, we subtracted the participant's mean Not asked
rating from each of their Asked ratings and compared these differences across
decisions with a mixed model. Because most "declined both" responses occurred
in Vignette 3, the own-baseline model was also refitted with a Decision ×
Vignette interaction, without Vignette 3, without participants whose decision
differed between their two Asked vignettes, and without the random intercept.
These analyses were not planned in advance and are correlational.

**Assumption checks and sensitivity analyses.** Residual and random-effect
distributions were inspected with Q–Q plots and residual-versus-fitted
plots. Because satisfaction was a single ordinal item, all satisfaction models
were refitted as cumulative link mixed models with a logit link (Christensen,
2026). The H2 model was also refitted without its single most extreme
observation.

**Software.** Analyses were conducted in R (Version 4.5.2; R Core Team, 2025)
using lme4 (Version 2.0.6; Bates et al., 2015) with Satterthwaite degrees of
freedom from lmerTest (Version 3.2.1; Kuznetsova et al., 2017), emmeans
(Version 2.0.4; Lenth, 2026), effectsize (Version 1.0.3; Ben-Shachar et al.,
2020), performance (Version 0.17.1; Lüdecke et al., 2021), and ordinal
(Version 2026.7.26; Christensen, 2026). Figures were created with ggplot2
(Wickham, 2016).

## Results

The analytic sample comprised 58 participants who each rated three vignettes
(174 observations). The cumulative link models for satisfaction led to the same
conclusions as the linear models in every case and are not reported further.

### Descriptive Statistics

Means and standard deviations by condition are shown in Table 1. Ratings fell
near the midpoint of the 1–5 scale, and the Asked and Not asked means differed
by no more than 0.03 points on any outcome.

**Table 1**

*Means and Standard Deviations of Outcomes by Condition*

| Outcome | Asked *M* (*SD*) | Not asked *M* (*SD*) | Overall *M* (*SD*) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Trust | 2.91 (0.83) | 2.94 (0.83) | 2.92 (0.83) |
| Acceptance | 3.28 (0.84) | 3.31 (0.78) | 3.29 (0.81) |
| Satisfaction | 3.27 (0.91) | 3.24 (0.87) | 3.26 (0.88) |

*Note.* Asked: 88 observations; Not asked: 86 observations, from 58
participants. All outcomes were rated on a 1–5 scale.

### Effect of Not Being Asked for Consent (H1)

**Between-participant comparisons.** Within each vignette, ratings of
participants who were not asked for consent did not differ significantly from
those of participants who were asked, for any outcome (Table 2). Across the nine
comparisons, |*t*|s ≤ 1.47, *p*s ≥ .148 (all Holm-adjusted *p*s = 1.00), and
effect sizes ranged from *g* = −0.22 to *g* = 0.38. Only five of the nine
differences were in the hypothesized direction; in Vignette 3, trust and
acceptance were nominally higher in the Not asked condition. Wilcoxon rank-sum
tests gave the same pattern (*p*s ≥ .171). With approximately 29 participants
per condition, these comparisons had 80% power only for differences of
*d* = 0.75 or larger.

**Table 2**

*Between-Participant Differences (Not Asked − Asked) by Vignette*

| Vignette | Outcome | *M*~diff~ [95% CI] | *t* (*df*) | *p* | Hedges' *g* [95% CI] |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Trust | −0.18 [−0.62, 0.25] | −0.84 (55.8) | .402 | −0.22 [−0.73, 0.29] |
| 1 | Acceptance | −0.12 [−0.54, 0.30] | −0.57 (55.5) | .568 | −0.15 [−0.66, 0.36] |
| 1 | Satisfaction | 0.03 [−0.39, 0.46] | 0.16 (56.0) | .872 | 0.04 [−0.47, 0.55] |
| 2 | Trust | −0.01 [−0.47, 0.44] | −0.06 (55.8) | .952 | −0.02 [−0.52, 0.49] |
| 2 | Acceptance | −0.09 [−0.53, 0.34] | −0.44 (55.9) | .663 | −0.11 [−0.62, 0.40] |
| 2 | Satisfaction | −0.14 [−0.63, 0.36] | −0.56 (55.3) | .578 | −0.15 [−0.65, 0.36] |
| 3 | Trust | 0.31 [−0.12, 0.73] | 1.44 (55.9) | .154 | 0.37 [−0.14, 0.88] |
| 3 | Acceptance | 0.31 [−0.11, 0.74] | 1.47 (54.0) | .148 | 0.38 [−0.13, 0.89] |
| 3 | Satisfaction | 0.02 [−0.47, 0.50] | 0.07 (54.1) | .945 | 0.02 [−0.49, 0.52] |

*Note.* Welch's *t* tests. Negative values indicate lower ratings in the Not
asked condition (the hypothesized direction). Holm-adjusted *p*s were 1.00 for
all comparisons.

**Within-participant effects.** Linear mixed models estimated the
within-person effect of not being asked, controlling for vignette and for each
participant's proportion of Not asked vignettes. Estimates were in the
hypothesized direction but small and not significant (Figure 1) for trust,
*b* = −0.03, *SE* = 0.06, 95% CI [−0.16, 0.09], *t*(113.0) = −0.52,
*p* = .602; acceptance, *b* = −0.05, *SE* = 0.08, 95% CI [−0.20, 0.10],
*t*(113.0) = −0.67, *p* = .507; or satisfaction, *b* = −0.10, *SE* = 0.10,
95% CI [−0.30, 0.11], *t*(113.0) = −0.92, *p* = .358 (all Holm-adjusted
*p*s = 1.00).

**Follow-up analyses.** Adding a Condition × Vignette interaction did not
significantly improve any model: trust, *F*(2, 125.4) = 0.47, *p* = .628;
acceptance, *F*(2, 135.1) = 2.96, *p* = .055; satisfaction,
*F*(2, 149.4) = 0.84, *p* = .435 (Holm-adjusted *p*s ≥ .165).

To assess whether the within-person effects were negligible rather than merely
non-significant, we conducted two one-sided tests (TOST; Lakens, 2017) on
the mixed-model estimates. [No smallest effect size of interest was
pre-specified; state the chosen bound and its justification here.] The 90%
CIs were [−0.14, 0.07] for trust, [−0.18, 0.08] for acceptance, and
[−0.27, 0.08] for satisfaction, so the effects were statistically equivalent
to zero for bounds of at least ±0.14, ±0.18, and ±0.27 scale points,
respectively (±0.16, ±0.22, and ±0.30 *SD*). With a bound of ±0.25 scale
points, equivalence was supported for trust (*p* < .001) and acceptance
(*p* = .006) but not for satisfaction (*p* = .068). With a bound of ±0.50 scale
points, equivalence was supported for all three outcomes (*p*s < .001).

Finally, we tested for carryover by adding the previous vignette's condition to
the within-participant models (Vignettes 2 and 3 only). The previous condition
did not predict trust, *b* = 0.03, 95% CI [−0.21, 0.26], *p* = .828;
acceptance, *b* = 0.13, 95% CI [−0.14, 0.41], *p* = .334; or satisfaction,
*b* = 0.00, 95% CI [−0.36, 0.36], *p* = .983, nor did it moderate the effect of
the current condition (*p*s ≥ .337). Because most participants switched
conditions between consecutive vignettes, current and previous condition were
negatively correlated (*r* = −.33), which reduces the precision of these
estimates.

In sum, H1 was not supported. Not being asked for consent did not lower trust,
acceptance, or satisfaction, either between participants within vignettes or
within participants across vignettes. Within participants, any such effect was
small: the CIs exclude decreases larger than 0.16 points for trust, 0.20 for
acceptance, and 0.30 for satisfaction.

### Trust and Acceptance as Predictors of Satisfaction (H2)

Satisfaction was regressed on the within- and between-person components of
trust and acceptance, controlling for condition and vignette. Entered
separately, trust predicted satisfaction both within participants,
*b* = 0.86, 95% CI [0.60, 1.13], *p* < .001, and between participants,
*b* = 0.71, 95% CI [0.55, 0.87], *p* < .001, as did acceptance (within:
*b* = 0.77, 95% CI [0.57, 0.98], *p* < .001; between: *b* = 0.90, 95% CI
[0.78, 1.02], *p* < .001).

When both predictors were entered together (Table 3 and Figure 2), within-person
fluctuations in both trust and acceptance uniquely predicted satisfaction.
Between participants, however, only acceptance remained a significant
predictor; trust did not explain satisfaction beyond acceptance. The fixed
effects explained 65.1% of the variance in satisfaction (marginal
*R*^2^; Nakagawa & Schielzeth, 2013) and the full model 67.7% (conditional
*R*^2^). Multicollinearity was moderate for the between-person components
(VIFs = 3.16–3.17) and low for the within-person components (VIFs = 1.55–1.56).
Excluding one observation with an unusually large residual (trust = 4.1,
acceptance = 4.0, satisfaction = 1) did not change any conclusion. H2 was
therefore supported, with acceptance the more consistent predictor.

**Table 3**

*Linear Mixed Model Predicting Satisfaction From Trust and Acceptance*

| Predictor | *b* | *SE* | 95% CI | *t* (*df*) | *p* |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Trust (within) | 0.46 | 0.15 | [0.16, 0.76] | 3.00 (111.2) | .003 |
| Trust (between) | 0.06 | 0.10 | [−0.14, 0.26] | 0.62 (55.0) | .540 |
| Acceptance (within) | 0.56 | 0.12 | [0.32, 0.80] | 4.55 (111.2) | < .001 |
| Acceptance (between) | 0.85 | 0.11 | [0.63, 1.06] | 7.86 (55.1) | < .001 |
| Not asked | −0.06 | 0.08 | [−0.21, 0.10] | −0.76 (131.4) | .450 |
| Vignette 2 | −0.08 | 0.10 | [−0.27, 0.12] | −0.78 (111.2) | .436 |
| Vignette 3 | −0.05 | 0.09 | [−0.24, 0.14] | −0.54 (111.2) | .593 |

*Note.* *N* = 174 observations from 58 participants; random intercept for
participant. Within = deviation from the participant's own mean; between =
participant mean across vignettes. Reference categories: Asked, Vignette 1.
Marginal *R*^2^ = .651, conditional *R*^2^ = .677.

### Exploratory Analyses: Consent Decisions

Among Asked vignettes, we explored whether ratings differed by participants'
responses to the two consent requests: consented to both (53 observations,
38 participants), consented to one (mixed; 22 observations, 19 participants),
or declined both (13 observations, 11 participants). Because participants
chose their responses, these analyses are correlational and were not
pre-specified.

Consent decision was associated with trust, *F*(2, 44.6) = 11.23,
*p* < .001; acceptance, *F*(2, 62.9) = 19.80, *p* < .001; and satisfaction,
*F*(2, 74.6) = 17.08, *p* < .001. Relative to participants who consented to
both requests, those who declined both gave lower ratings of trust,
*b* = −0.70, 95% CI [−1.06, −0.34]; acceptance, *b* = −1.21, 95% CI
[−1.66, −0.76]; and satisfaction, *b* = −1.33, 95% CI [−1.87, −0.78]
(Holm-adjusted *p*s < .001). Mixed decisions fell in between (trust:
*b* = −0.32, *p* = .013; acceptance: *b* = −0.45, *p* = .005; satisfaction:
*b* = −0.60, *p* = .002; Holm-adjusted within outcome).

These differences appeared to reflect, in large part, participants' general
stance toward MedHelper. Participants' consent rate (the proportion of requests
accepted) also predicted their ratings in the vignettes in which they were
*not* asked: trust, *b* = 0.96, 95% CI [0.39, 1.53], *p* = .001; acceptance,
*b* = 0.64, 95% CI [0.08, 1.21], *p* = .027; satisfaction, *b* = 0.80, 95% CI
[0.27, 1.33], *p* = .004. A Consent Rate × Condition interaction tested
whether this gap was larger in Asked than in Not asked vignettes. The gap was
numerically larger when participants were asked, but not significantly so:
trust, *b* = 0.22, 95% CI [−0.15, 0.59], *p* = .249; acceptance, *b* = 0.36,
95% CI [−0.10, 0.81], *p* = .127; satisfaction, *b* = 0.21, 95% CI
[−0.40, 0.82], *p* = .502 (Holm-adjusted *p*s ≥ .382). The CIs nonetheless
allow for a moderate additional effect of the decision, so it cannot be ruled
out.

**Distance from the Not asked condition.** Figure 3 shows mean ratings for
each consent status. For every outcome, participants who consented to both
requests rated at or above the Not asked mean, and those who declined both
rated below it. At the group level, the gap between Not asked and "declined
both" ratings was larger than the gap between Not asked and "consented to
both" ratings by 0.66 points for trust, 95% CI [0.11, 1.22], *p* = .020; 0.76
for acceptance, 95% CI [0.12, 1.40], *p* = .021; and 0.63 for satisfaction,
95% CI [−0.07, 1.33], *p* = .075. None of these differences remained
significant after Holm correction (adjusted *p*s ≥ .060).

Relative to their own Not asked ratings, participants rated higher in
vignettes where they consented to both requests (trust: 0.16, 95% CI
[0.03, 0.30]; acceptance: 0.29, 95% CI [0.10, 0.47]; satisfaction: 0.29, 95%
CI [0.07, 0.52]). They rated lower where they declined both (trust: −0.17,
95% CI [−0.40, 0.07]; acceptance: −0.40, 95% CI [−0.75, −0.05]; satisfaction:
−0.36, 95% CI [−0.79, 0.06]). The two gaps were of similar size
(differences in absolute gap 0.00–0.12 points, *p*s ≥ .574), so the larger
group-level gap to decliners mainly reflected decliners being lower raters in
general. However, ratings in a vignette where the participant declined were
lower relative to their own baseline than ratings where they consented: trust,
*b* = −0.33, 95% CI [−0.59, −0.07], *p* = .013; acceptance, *b* = −0.69,
95% CI [−1.07, −0.31], *p* < .001; satisfaction, *b* = −0.66, 95% CI
[−1.13, −0.19], *p* = .007 (Holm-adjusted *p*s ≤ .014). Taken at face value,
this suggests that the decision was associated with ratings of that
particular vignette, beyond the participant's general stance.

This vignette-specific association was not robust. Eight of the 13 "declined
both" ratings came from Vignette 3. The association did not differ
significantly across vignettes (Decision × Vignette interaction, *p*s ≥ .564),
but with only two and three "declined both" ratings in Vignettes 1 and 2, this
test had little power. When the Vignette 3 "declined both" ratings were
removed, the differences kept their direction (−0.34 to −0.53 points) but
were not significant for any outcome (*p*s = .069–.185). Removing Vignette 3
altogether left only acceptance significant (*b* = −0.70, *p* < .001), an
estimate based on five "declined both" ratings. The estimates rested largely
on the 10 participants whose decision differed between their two Asked
vignettes, for whom declined and consented ratings could be compared within
the same person. Of the five such participants who declined both requests in
one vignette, four did so in Vignette 3. Without these 10 participants, the
differences shrank to −0.11 to −0.27 points (*p*s ≥ .286). Weighting all
observations equally (no random intercept, cluster-robust standard errors)
gave differences of −0.19 to −0.42 points, significant only for acceptance
(*p* = .018; Holm-adjusted *p* = .053). The evidence for a vignette-specific
association between declining and lower ratings therefore rests on a small
number of participants, most of whom declined in Vignette 3. Like the other
exploratory results, it is correlational: a participant who disliked a
particular scenario may have declined consent because of it.
